# TxStream: Lanes, Batching & Throughput

Source: https://cardano-client.dev/txstream/throughput/
Summary: The UTXO concurrency model: lane policies, windows, planners, partitioned fan-out, and honest throughput expectations

:::caution[Experimental]
TxStream is experimental, and its APIs and behaviour may change. See [known issues](/project/known-issues/#txstream) before relying on it.
:::

Cardano's eUTXO model *is* TxStream's concurrency model. Two transactions that spend disjoint
UTXOs can be in flight simultaneously; two transactions spending the same funds cannot. TxStream
expresses that directly:

- A **lane** is a funding scope — a funding address or funding reference whose UTXOs at most one
  in-flight execution may spend at a time.
- **Different lanes run concurrently; the same lane runs serial FIFO.** Throughput scales with
  the number of disjoint funding scopes, not with thread counts.
- Scheduling keys on the lane's **canonical spending identity, never its display name**: two lane
  labels resolving to the same wallet are one lane wearing two names and share one FIFO. Labels
  can never be used to sneak two writers onto one wallet.
- The lane also constrains **coin selection**: an item's transaction is mechanically pinned to its
  lane's funding scope (violations fail typed `TXSTREAM_LANE_SCOPE_VIOLATION`), and the lane is
  declared as the engine's spending resource — the cross-process safety net if another process
  ever runs against the same funds. Template items are exempt from the pin: keep each template's
  `from_ref` equal to its lane's source yourself.

> **Alias caveat:** for funding-*ref* lanes, identity is the reference string as given
> (`ref:account://sender`), caller-asserted canonical. Two different references naming the same
> wallet — or a ref lane and an address lane over the same wallet — are treated as distinct lanes
> today; keeping such aliases from running concurrently is your responsibility.

## Lane policies

| Policy | Lane comes from | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LanePolicy.single(lane)` / builder `.lane(...)` | one static configuration | One funding wallet, strict FIFO — the simplest correct start |
| `LanePolicy.explicit()` + `laneResolver` | each item's `withLane(name)` | You route work to named funding scopes (treasury vs operations) |
| `LanePolicy.byFundingSource()` (default) | each item's own `from`/`from_ref` | Items already carry their funding source; senders lane themselves |
| `LanePolicy.partitioned(config)` | `hash(idempotencyKey) % N` over N app-owned addresses | Maximum throughput from one logical wallet — see the deep-dive below |

**Explicit lanes** resolve names through a required `LaneIdentityResolver`, once per name at first
use. An item without a lane fails typed `TXSTREAM_LANE_REQUIRED`; an unresolvable name fails that
item typed `TXSTREAM_LANE_UNRESOLVED` (it cannot be a startup error — names arrive with items):

```java
try (TxFlowStream stream = TxFlowStream.builder("payouts", engine)
        .lanes(LanePolicy.explicit())
        .laneResolver(laneName -> {
            switch (laneName) {
                case "treasury":
                    return ResolvedLane.ofFundingRef("treasury", "account://treasury");
                case "operations":
                    return ResolvedLane.ofFundingRef("operations", "account://operations");
                default:
                    return null;   // fails the item typed TXSTREAM_LANE_UNRESOLVED
            }
        })
        .maxInFlight(8)
        .executor(streamExecutor)
        .open()) {
    stream.submit(TxWorkItem.builder("treasury-pay-1")
            .withTxPlan(treasuryPlan)
            .withLane("treasury")
            .build());
    stream.submit(TxWorkItem.builder("ops-pay-1")
            .withTxPlan(opsPlan)
            .withLane("operations")   // different identity: runs concurrently
            .build());
}
```

**Funding-address-derived lanes** need no resolver and no per-item lane name — the transaction's
own funding source is the lane, so same-sender items serialize and different senders parallelize
for free. An item whose transaction names no funding source fails typed
`TXSTREAM_LANE_UNDERIVABLE`; an item that names a lane must name the derived one or fails
`TXSTREAM_LANE_MISMATCH` (that last rule applies under `single(...)` too — a lane name is never a
silent label):

```java
TxFlowStream stream = TxFlowStream.builder("payouts", engine).open();
```

The default policy is `byFundingSource()`; the builder call is only needed when making the choice
explicit. `byFundingAddress()` remains a deprecated compatibility alias. Dispatch inherits the
engine execution executor unless overridden; give an explicit stream executor at least as many
threads as the number of lanes you want concurrently dispatching.

## Windows and planners

By default there is no windowing and the `perItem()` planner plans every accepted item
immediately as its own single-step flow — maximum lane parallelism, true per-item idempotency.
Multi-item planning is opt-in via a `WindowPolicy` plus a planner:

- `WindowPolicy.count(n)` — close the window at n items; no timer needed.
- `WindowPolicy.countOrTime(n, maxAge)` — n items or the oldest item's age, whichever first.
- `WindowPolicy.time(maxAge)` — age only.

Time-based policies need a scheduler. Set `maintenanceExecutor(ScheduledExecutorService)`, or let the stream inherit the engine's maintenance executor when it's a `ScheduledExecutorService`: the
stream owns no threads or timers, so window-age wakeups run on your scheduler (one scheduled
wakeup per open window).

```java
ScheduledExecutorService maintenance = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor();

TxFlowStream perWindowStream = TxFlowStream.builder("payouts-window", engine)
        .lane(ResolvedLane.ofFundingRef("payouts", "account://sender"))
        .planner(TxStreamPlanner.perWindow())
        .window(WindowPolicy.countOrTime(50, Duration.ofSeconds(10)))
        .maintenanceExecutor(maintenance)   // a scheduler for time-based windows
        .executor(streamExecutor)
        .build();

TxFlowStream batchingStream = TxFlowStream.builder("payouts-batch", engine)
        .lane(ResolvedLane.ofFundingRef("payouts", "account://sender"))
        .planner(TxStreamPlanner.batching(BatchingOptions.builder()
                .maxItemsPerTransaction(20)
                .allowNonPaymentSingletons(true)
                .build()))
        .window(WindowPolicy.count(20))
        .executor(streamExecutor)
        .build();
```

The three built-in planners:

- **`perItem()`** (default) — one single-step flow per item. The only planner with per-item
  exactly-once; sources that redeliver individual items should use this one.
- **`perWindow()`** — one shared flow per *lane group* in the window; each item rides its own
  step (its own transaction) of the shared execution. Fewer engine executions, per-item
  transactions preserved. Flow-level dedup only. `perWindow(ChainingMode.PIPELINED)` opts into
  same-lane pipelining: each generated step may fund from every earlier same-lane step's unspent,
  matching-address pending outputs. `SEQUENTIAL` is the default; `BATCH` is not supported here.
- **`batching(options)`** — merges compatible payment-shaped items within a lane group into
  **one** transaction (one flow, one merged step; overflow beyond `maxItemsPerTransaction`
  splits into further merged flows). Fewer on-chain transactions and lower total fees; merged
  members share one fate — the batch confirms or fails together:

```java
TxStreamItemResult a = first.completion().toCompletableFuture().join();
TxStreamItemResult b = second.completion().toCompletableFuture().join();
// Merged members share one transaction, one execution, one step:
boolean merged = a.getTransactionHash().equals(b.getTransactionHash())
        && a.getExecutionId().equals(b.getExecutionId())
        && a.getStepId().equals(b.getStepId());

Optional<TxStreamBatchResult> batch = stream.getBatchStatus("batch-1");
batch.ifPresent(result -> System.out.println(result.status()
        + " executions=" + result.executionIds()));
```

> **What is NOT batchable, and what merging drops.** Only pure payments merge: an item carrying a
> script, mint, staking, governance, metadata, `collectFrom`, reference inputs, or a
> contract/datum-bearing output is not payment-shaped and runs unmerged as its own single-item
> flow (or fails the window typed, with `allowNonPaymentSingletons(false)`). The merged
> transaction is a minimal reconstruction from the members' payment outputs plus the lane's
> funding source — **per-member transaction context is not carried**: extra signers, custom fee
> payer, change address, and validity windows are dropped. Items needing any of that belong
> under `perItem()` or `perWindow()`.
>
> **Batching needs a funding-ref lane.** A merged plan gets a signer only on a funding-ref lane
> (`ofFundingRef` or `from_ref`). On an address lane the merged transaction has no signer, so the
> batch fails with `No signers found` and no funds move.

> **Dedup warning:** `perWindow()` and `batching(...)` provide flow-level dedup only, and under
> batching a re-batched payment is a **real second on-chain payment**. Read
> [dedup scopes](/txstream/durability/#dedup-scopes-what-exactly-once-actually-covers) before
> using either with a redelivering source.

Custom planners implement `TxStreamPlanner` — plan a closed window into executions, deriving flow
and step ids from the context's `StableIdFactory` (determinism is an SPI obligation: the same
items must produce a byte-identical plan, or redeliveries become `TXFLOW_IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT`
failures). Plans are validated before dispatch (`TXSTREAM_PLAN_INVALID`,
`TXSTREAM_PLAN_CROSS_LANE`); a planner that throws fails only that window's items
(`TXSTREAM_PLANNER_FAILED`), never the stream.

## Partitioned lanes: the fan-out deep-dive

Items may use QuickTx extensions registered on the engine (`FlowEngine.Builder.extension` or
`FlowRuntime.Builder.extension`). An unregistered extension is rejected at submit with
`TXSTREAM_NON_PORTABLE_ITEM`, `batching(...)` never merges extension items, and `perWindow()` splits
items with conflicting bindings into separate flows on the same lane.

`LanePolicy.partitioned(...)` is the full UTXO throughput story for a single logical wallet: the
funding source is split across N lane addresses, items are assigned by `hash(idempotencyKey) % N`
(stable across restarts), and the N lanes run concurrently — throughput scales with N, not block
time.

:::caution[Pre-fund your lanes in this preview]
The built-in bootstrap transaction carries no signer, so `bootstrap(true)` fails `start()` with
`TXSTREAM_BOOTSTRAP_FAILED`. Fund the lane addresses yourself and use `bootstrap(false)`.
:::

Items must leave `from` and `from_ref` unset, or name exactly their assigned lane address; otherwise
they fail `TXSTREAM_LANE_SCOPE_VIOLATION`. A plan's signers must be able to sign for whichever lane
the hash assigns:

```java
PartitionedLanes partitioning = PartitionedLanes.fromRef("account://treasury")
        .laneAddresses(laneAddresses)       // order is stability-critical
        .seedPerLane(Amount.ada(200))
        .bootstrap(false)                   // lanes are already funded
        .build();

TxFlowStream stream = TxFlowStream.builder("payouts-partitioned", durableEngine)
        .lanes(LanePolicy.partitioned(partitioning))
        .stateStore(TxStreamStateStore.inMemoryDurable())  // durable: drift fails fast
        .executor(streamExecutor)
        .build();
stream.start();

TxPlan plan = TxPlan.from(new Tx().payToAddress(receiver, Amount.ada(2)))
        .withSigner("account://lane0")
        .withSigner("account://lane1");
stream.submit("payout-1", plan).awaitConfirmed(Duration.ofMinutes(5));
```

With `bootstrap(false)` the lanes are assumed pre-funded. Min-ADA per lane and
consolidating lanes on shutdown are the caller's economics — the stream never manages keys.

> **FUNDS-CRITICAL: the partitioned configuration must be byte-stable across restarts.** The
> funding source, the per-lane seed, the lane count N, and the lane-address list **including its
> order** all feed the bootstrap's idempotency claim — changing any of them mints a *new* claim,
> i.e. a new split that **re-drains the funding wallet**; and the address order additionally
> defines the `partitionIndex → lane` mapping, so reordering remaps every item's lane even with N
> and the addresses unchanged. A **durable** partitioned stream persists the bootstrap
> fingerprint and fails `start()` typed (`TXSTREAM_BOOTSTRAP_CONFIG_DRIFT`) on any drift, before
> submitting a split. A **non-durable** stream has nowhere to persist the fingerprint and
> **cannot detect drift — it will silently re-split**. Run partitioned streams durable unless you
> are certain the configuration is generated deterministically.

Template items currently require an explicit lane (`single` or `explicit`); under
`byFundingSource()`/`partitioned(...)` they fail typed `TXSTREAM_LANE_REQUIRED`.

## Honest throughput expectations

What the current built-ins actually deliver:

- **Lanes are real parallelism** — N disjoint funding scopes give up to N concurrent in-flight
  executions (devnet-validated), bounded by `maxInFlight`.
- **Batching is real transaction reduction** — up to `maxItemsPerTransaction` payments per
  on-chain transaction (devnet-validated: two payments merged into one transaction).
- **Within one flow, `perWindow()` is SEQUENTIAL by default**: a flow of 50 items confirms its 50
  steps one at a time, and a lane running `perItem()` flows waits for each item's confirmation
  before dispatching the next. `perWindow(ChainingMode.PIPELINED)` with a `WindowPolicy` submits a
  window's steps without waiting for confirmation between them. The lane still runs one execution
  at a time, so the next window waits for the current one, and windows of one gain nothing. Dedup
  stays flow-level.

So today's levers, in order: **more lanes** (explicit or partitioned), then **batching** (fewer,
larger transactions), then `perWindow(PIPELINED)` with window sizing. If a lane must exceed roughly one transaction per
confirmation interval and batching cannot absorb it, that is the signal to partition further.

## Feeding a stream from java.util.concurrent.Flow

For reactive pipelines, `TxWorkSource.fromPublisher(...)` bridges a `Flow.Publisher<TxWorkItem>`
with real demand-based backpressure: the adapter prefetches a bounded number of items (default
64), requests one more as each accepted item settles, and parks items while the buffer is full or
the stream is an ownership standby (`PAUSED`) — items are never dropped and demand is never
unbounded. `TxStreamFlowPublisher` is the outbound half: an event listener that publishes item
results to `Flow` subscribers.

```java
SubmissionPublisher<TxWorkItem> publisher = new SubmissionPublisher<>();
FlowWorkSource source = TxWorkSource.fromPublisher(publisher, 64);

TxStreamFlowPublisher results = TxStreamFlowPublisher.terminalOnly();

try (TxFlowStream stream = TxFlowStream.builder("payouts-reactive", engine)
        .lane(ResolvedLane.ofFundingRef("payouts", "account://sender"))
        .source(source)
        .eventListener(results)
        .executor(streamExecutor)
        .build()) {
    results.subscribe(resultSubscriber);   // Flow.Subscriber<TxStreamItemResult>
    stream.start();

    publisher.submit(TxWorkItem.builder("pay-1")
            .withTxPlan(plan)
            .build());
    publisher.close();

    source.terminated().toCompletableFuture().join();   // publisher finished
    stream.drain();                                     // accepted work settles
}
```

> **Subscribers must not block in `onNext` (Reactive Streams §2.2).** Delivery is inline on the
> stream's callback thread — the thread that advanced the item's projection. A subscriber that
> blocks inside `onNext` stalls that lane's further dispatch (other lanes, other subscribers, and
> the item's own `completion()` are unaffected). A merely *slow* (under-requesting) subscriber is
> different and safe: its bounded buffer (default 256) overflows and it is terminated with
> `TxStreamSubscriberOverflowException` and dropped — it never back-pressures the stream.

## Scalability notes

- **`maxInFlight`** (default 16) caps concurrent executions across all lanes, on top of the
  one-per-lane rule. Ready lanes are scheduled round-robin, so one lane's backlog cannot starve
  the others.
- **Lane maps are unbounded.** Resolved lane identities and their FIFO state are retained for the
  stream's lifetime. Under `byFundingSource()` with high-cardinality senders (many thousands of
  distinct funding addresses through one stream), that map grows without bound — prefer a bounded
  set of explicit or partitioned lanes for that shape.
- **`maxBufferSize`** (default 1000) bounds accepted-but-undispatched items; `submit` blocks and
  `trySubmit` reports `FULL` when it is reached. A count-only window larger than the buffer is
  rejected at `build()` (it could never fill).
- One stream instance per lane set: sharing a lane's funding scope across processes without
  ownership mode is out of scope until the engine's cross-process busy-claim path lands; the
  engine's spending-resource coordination is the safety net, not a throughput feature.

## Continue

- [TxStream Getting Started](/txstream/getting-started/) — item identity, receipts, lifecycle.
- [TxStream: Durability & Exactly-Once](/txstream/durability/) — dedup scopes (mandatory reading
  for `perWindow()`/`batching()`), re-attach, and HA.

## Backend indexing and qualification

Confirmation and UTxO indexing can become visible at different times. Backend-based
engines enable TxStream's between-execution output-visibility check by default. It
holds the lane until the preceding transaction's output zero is queryable, bounded
by the stream's `backendVisibility(timeout, pollInterval)` budget. A timeout fails
new work before engine start with `TXSTREAM_BACKEND_NOT_READY`; the preceding
transaction remains confirmed or uncertain as previously reported.

Custom four-supplier engines must opt in with `backendVisibilityChecks(true)` and
provide historical output lookup. This check does not establish atomic consistency
across all provider endpoints or coordinate unrelated spenders. Measure both
confirmation and indexing delay with the provider used in deployment.

The soak runner also has its own application submission gate. Report gated and
ungated runs separately; a gated throughput result must not be presented as a
measurement of the ordinary SDK submission path. Preview qualification should
include delayed indexing, unavailable output lookups, and consecutive same-lane
payments without that application gate.

Backend visibility retries release the worker and in-flight slot between probes.
`FlowRuntime` supplies the retry scheduler. Direct stream builders inherit the
engine's maintenance executor when it implements `ScheduledExecutorService`;
an explicit stream `maintenanceExecutor(...)` takes precedence. When neither
provides a scheduler, an unsuccessful probe fails before engine start. A plain
`Executor` cannot schedule retries. Plain `close()` keeps retries active while
it drains and cancels remaining timers afterward; abort cancels them immediately.
Parked executions retain their buffer permits, so `maxBufferSize` includes them.
The pending hashes are process-local and reset
on restart; authoritative FAILED/CANCELLED repair clears the affected item's hold.
A visibility timeout fails every member of the waiting execution. Their IDs remain
registered. Because this particular error proves the engine never started, the
caller may retry that work under new IDs; this does not apply to RECOVERY_REQUIRED.
Custom backend-based engines used by TxStream enable visibility checks by default;
custom output services must support historical output lookup or explicitly disable
`backendVisibilityChecks`. Ordinary engine executions do not invoke this stream gate.

---

# Jellyfish Merkle Tree

Source: https://cardano-client.dev/verified-structures/jmt/
Summary: Versioned, authenticated off-chain state with inclusion and absence proofs.

> **Preview feature**: available in the [latest preview](/start-here/installation/#versions). APIs may change before the stable release.

A Jellyfish Merkle Tree (JMT) keeps every version of your state, so you can read and prove a key as of any version. Each commit is one batch of updates with a version number. It's inspired by Diem's JMT, but its commitments and proofs aren't compatible with Diem or Aptos.

There's no on-chain verifier, and keys can't be deleted. If a validator needs to check proofs, [use MPF](/verified-structures/mpf/). The supported production scope is serialized off-chain state with one logical writer per namespace.

## Quick start

Add the [dependency](/verified-structures/overview/#dependencies), then:

```java
import com.bloxbean.cardano.vds.jmt.JellyfishMerkleTree;
import com.bloxbean.cardano.vds.jmt.rocksdb.RocksDbJmtStore;

try (RocksDbJmtStore store = new RocksDbJmtStore("data/jmt")) {
    JellyfishMerkleTree tree = new JellyfishMerkleTree(store);

    // Version 1
    Map<byte[], byte[]> updates = new HashMap<>();
    updates.put("alice".getBytes(), "balance:100".getBytes());
    updates.put("bob".getBytes(), "balance:200".getBytes());
    tree.put(1L, updates);

    // Version 2
    JellyfishMerkleTree.CommitResult commit =
            tree.put(2L, Map.of("alice".getBytes(), "balance:150".getBytes()));
    byte[] rootV2 = commit.rootHash();

    Optional<byte[]> latest = tree.get("alice".getBytes());        // "balance:150"
    Optional<byte[]> old = tree.get("alice".getBytes(), 1L);       // "balance:100"
}
```

For tests, `InMemoryJmtStore` works without any storage module.

Put many updates in one commit rather than committing each key on its own: batching normally reduces storage and rewriting.

## Versions

- New versions must increase. Gaps are allowed, and writing below the latest version throws `IllegalArgumentException`.
- `get(key, version)` answers *as of* that version, so a version between two commits reads the earlier commit.
- `get(key, version)` throws `IllegalArgumentException` for a version newer than the latest commit, or below the prune watermark. It doesn't fall back to some other state.
- `getProof(key, version)` needs a root committed at exactly that version, and returns empty otherwise.

If your position can be ahead of the latest commit, such as a chain tip that skipped empty blocks, read at `min(position, store.latestRoot().get().version())`.

## Proofs

`getProof` returns an inclusion proof for a key that exists and an absence proof for one that doesn't.

```java
JmtProfile profile = JmtProfile.classicBlake2b256V1();

JmtProof proof = tree.getProof("alice".getBytes(), 2L).orElseThrow();
boolean included = JmtProofVerifier.verify(rootV2, "alice".getBytes(), proof.value(), proof,
        profile.hashFunction(), profile.commitmentScheme());

// value() is null for an absence proof, and null asks the verifier to check absence
JmtProof absence = tree.getProof("nobody".getBytes(), 2L).orElseThrow();
boolean absent = JmtProofVerifier.verify(rootV2, "nobody".getBytes(), null, absence,
        profile.hashFunction(), profile.commitmentScheme());
```

The verifier returns true only when the proof shows exactly that statement: an inclusion proof never proves absence, and an absence proof never proves a value.

To send a proof over the network, use CBOR:

```java
byte[] wire = tree.getProofWire("alice".getBytes(), 2L).orElseThrow();
boolean valid = tree.verifyProofWire(rootV2, "alice".getBytes(), "balance:150".getBytes(), true, wire);
```

## Pruning

```java
int removed = tree.pruneUpTo(2L);
OptionalLong watermark = store.pruneWatermark();
```

The watermark is the greatest committed version at or below the horizon. Its state stays readable and provable. Reads and proofs below it are rejected, and `truncateAfter` below it throws `IllegalStateException`.

With the RocksDB `AGGRESSIVE` value-prune policy, the watermark moves to the latest version at prune time, because that policy drops older values of rewritten keys.

## Thread safety

Competing writes to a namespace fail immediately with `JmtConcurrentMutationException`. Pruning and rollback are exclusive and fail fast if a read or update is active. Every tree or store wrapper for a namespace must share one coordinator, and PostgreSQL also enforces the single writer across processes.

## Format

Persistent stores record the `classic-radix16-blake2b256-v1` format and refuse to open incompatible data. The deprecated `JellyfishMerkleTree(store, hashFn)` constructors are for in-memory stores only: RocksDB and SQL stores reject them with `JmtFormatMismatchException`.

For metrics, the design and the production checklist, see the [module README](https://github.com/bloxbean/cardano-client-lib/tree/master/verified-structures/jellyfish-merkle).

---

# MpfTrie

Source: https://cardano-client.dev/verified-structures/mpf/
Summary: Merkle Patricia Forestry on RocksDB, with proofs that Aiken validators can verify.

> **Preview feature**: available in the [latest preview](/start-here/installation/#versions). APIs may change before the stable release.

`MpfTrie` is the off-chain counterpart of Aiken's [merkle-patricia-forestry](https://github.com/aiken-lang/merkle-patricia-forestry) library. Its roots and proofs are identical to those of the library's official JavaScript implementation.

It uses Blake2b-256 and CBOR, so its proofs don't work with Ethereum's Merkle Patricia tries.

## Quick start

Add the [dependency](/verified-structures/overview/#dependencies), then:

```java
import com.bloxbean.cardano.vds.mpf.MpfTrie;
import com.bloxbean.cardano.vds.mpf.rocksdb.RocksDbMptSession;
import com.bloxbean.cardano.vds.mpf.rocksdb.RocksDbStateTrees;

try (RocksDbStateTrees stateTrees = new RocksDbStateTrees("data/mpf")) {
    MpfTrie trie = new MpfTrie(stateTrees.nodeStore());
    RocksDbMptSession session = RocksDbMptSession.of(stateTrees);

    // One atomic batch: trie nodes, version entry and refcounts
    session.write(() -> {
        trie.put("alice".getBytes(), "100".getBytes());
        trie.put("bob".getBytes(), "200".getBytes());
        return stateTrees.putRootWithRefcount(trie.getRootHash());
    });

    byte[] value = trie.get("alice".getBytes());     // "100"
    byte[] rootForDatum = trie.getRootHashOrEmpty(); // store this on chain
}
```

Keys are hashed before they're stored, so you can look up a key or iterate over all entries, but you can't query by prefix or range.

## Reopen a trie

```java
try (RocksDbStateTrees stateTrees = new RocksDbStateTrees("data/mpf")) {
    MpfTrie trie = new MpfTrie(stateTrees.nodeStore(), stateTrees.rootsIndex().latest());
    byte[] value = trie.get("alice".getBytes());
}
```

When the root comes from an on-chain datum, use `MpfTrie.open(store, root)`, available from 0.8.0-pre7. It throws `IllegalStateException` if the store doesn't have that root. The constructors are lenient: with an unknown root, reads return `null` and the next `put` starts a new trie.

## The empty trie

`getRootHash()` returns `null` for an empty trie, while Aiken's `mpf.empty` root is 32 zero bytes. For datums, use `getRootHashOrEmpty()`, available from 0.8.0-pre7, which returns those zero bytes. `new MpfTrie(store, <32 zero bytes>)` and `MpfTrie.open(store, <32 zero bytes>)` both open an empty trie.

## Proofs for Aiken

```java
byte[] key = "alice".getBytes();
byte[] value = trie.get(key);
byte[] root = trie.getRootHash();

// Ready to use in a redeemer, as Aiken's `Proof` type
ListPlutusData proof = trie.getProofPlutusData(key).orElseThrow();

// The same proof as wire CBOR, with off-chain checks
byte[] wire = trie.getProofWire(key).orElseThrow();
boolean present = trie.verifyProofWire(root, key, value, true, wire);

byte[] missing = "carol".getBytes();
byte[] missingWire = trie.getProofWire(missing).orElseThrow();
boolean absent = trie.verifyProofWire(root, missing, null, false, missingWire);
```

`verifyProofWire` returns `false` for a malformed proof and never throws. To verify without a trie, use `ProofVerifier.verify(root, key, value, including, wire)`.

A key's proof depends on the trie you take it from, and one proof serves several Aiken operations:

| Aiken call | Take the proof of `key` from |
|---|---|
| `mpf.has(trie, key, value, proof)` | The trie that contains `key` |
| `mpf.miss(trie, key, proof)` | The trie that doesn't contain `key` |
| `mpf.insert(trie, key, value, proof)` | The trie before the insert, or after it |
| `mpf.delete(trie, key, value, proof)` | The trie before the delete, or after it |
| `mpf.update(trie, key, proof, old, new)` | The trie before the update |

:::danger[Validators that use `miss` or `insert`]
`aiken-lang/merkle-patricia-forestry` 2.1.0 doesn't check the shape of proof steps, or that a terminal `Leaf` or `Fork` neighbor differs from the queried key. With a crafted proof, `mpf.miss` accepts a key that is present, and `mpf.insert` accepts re-inserting a present key with a new value. We reproduced both with `aiken check`.

CCL never produces such proofs and `verifyProofWire` rejects them, but on-chain code doesn't. If your validator relies on `miss` or `insert` to enforce absence or uniqueness, also check every step of the redeemer proof: `Fork` nibble and prefix bytes in 0..15, 32-byte `root`, `key` and `value`, and a neighbor nibble that differs from the key's nibble at that position.
:::

The same proof can be encoded several ways, and `verifyProofWire` accepts all of them. Don't use proof bytes or their hash as an identifier; use the key and the root.

## Upgrading from 0.8.0-pre6 or earlier

Proofs changed in 0.8.0-pre7, so **regenerate stored proofs**:

- Earlier exclusion proofs ending in a `Fork` step were rejected by Aiken, and they now fail `verifyProofWire` too. Older CCL versions reject the new ones.
- Earlier inclusion proofs used only `Branch` steps. Aiken accepts those for `has` and `update` but not for `delete`. They still pass `verifyProofWire`.

Tries written by 0.8.0-pre6 still open with identical roots and values. See [garbage collection](/verified-structures/multi-version-gc/) if you ran GC on them.

## API

```java
// Constructors (lenient) and strict factory
MpfTrie(NodeStore store)
MpfTrie(NodeStore store, byte[] rootHash)
MpfTrie(NodeStore store, HashFunction hashFn)             // not Aiken-compatible
static MpfTrie open(NodeStore store, byte[] rootHash)     // fails if the root isn't in the store

// Core operations
void put(byte[] key, byte[] value)
byte[] get(byte[] key)
void delete(byte[] key)
byte[] getRootHash()                                      // null for an empty trie
byte[] getRootHashOrEmpty()                               // all zeros for an empty trie
void setRootHash(byte[] root)

// Proofs
Optional<byte[]> getProofWire(byte[] key)
Optional<ListPlutusData> getProofPlutusData(byte[] key)
boolean verifyProofWire(byte[] root, byte[] key, byte[] value, boolean including, byte[] wire)

// Introspection
List<Entry> getAllEntries()
List<Entry> getEntries(int limit)
TrieStatistics getStatistics()
int computeSize()
String printTree()
```

`MpfTrie` isn't thread-safe, and the storage backends don't coordinate concurrent writers. Use one writer per trie.

For more, see the [module README](https://github.com/bloxbean/cardano-client-lib/tree/master/verified-structures/merkle-patricia-forestry).

---

# MPF versions and garbage collection

Source: https://cardano-client.dev/verified-structures/multi-version-gc/
Summary: Record versions of an MpfTrie on RocksDB, read old versions and reclaim space.

> **Preview feature**: available in the [latest preview](/start-here/installation/#versions). APIs may change before the stable release.

## Record versions

`RocksDbStateTrees` defaults to `StorageMode.MULTI_VERSION`. The mode is saved on first open and checked on every later open. The SQL backend defaults to `SINGLE_VERSION`, so pass the mode explicitly if you might use both.

```java
try (RocksDbStateTrees stateTrees = new RocksDbStateTrees("data/mpf")) {
    MpfTrie trie = new MpfTrie(stateTrees.nodeStore());
    RocksDbMptSession session = RocksDbMptSession.of(stateTrees);

    long v1 = session.write(() -> {
        trie.put("alice".getBytes(), "100".getBytes());
        return stateTrees.putRootWithRefcount(trie.getRootHash());
    });

    long v2 = session.write(() -> {
        trie.put("alice".getBytes(), "150".getBytes());
        return stateTrees.putRootWithRefcount(trie.getRootHash());
    });

    // Read an older version
    MpfTrie atV1 = new MpfTrie(stateTrees.nodeStore(), stateTrees.rootsIndex().get(v1));
    byte[] alice = atV1.get("alice".getBytes());   // "100"
}
```

If you collect garbage with mark-sweep only, `stateTrees.rootsIndex().put(version, root)` is enough to record a version.

## Keep only the latest state

```java
try (RocksDbStateTrees stateTrees = new RocksDbStateTrees("data/mpf", StorageMode.SINGLE_VERSION)) {
    MpfTrie trie = new MpfTrie(stateTrees.nodeStore(), stateTrees.getCurrentRoot());
    trie.put("alice".getBytes(), "100".getBytes());
    stateTrees.putRootSnapshot(trie.getRootHash());   // overwrites version 0
    stateTrees.cleanupOrphanedNodes(new GcOptions()); // keeps only the current root
}
```

## Garbage collection

Every `put` writes new nodes and leaves the old ones in place. GC deletes the nodes that no retained version reaches.

```java
import com.bloxbean.cardano.vds.mpf.rocksdb.gc.*;
import com.bloxbean.cardano.vds.mpf.rocksdb.gc.strategy.*;

GcManager gc = new GcManager(stateTrees.nodeStore(), stateTrees.rootsIndex());

GcOptions options = new GcOptions();
options.deleteBatchSize = 10_000;
options.progress = deleted -> System.out.println("deleted " + deleted);

GcReport report = gc.runSync(new OnDiskMarkSweepStrategy(), RetentionPolicy.keepLatestN(5), options);
System.out.println("deleted " + report.deleted + " of " + report.total + " nodes");
```

`runSync` declares `throws Exception`. To simulate a run, set `options.dryRun = true`. `gc.runAsync(strategy, policy, options, report -> ...)` runs on a daemon thread and passes the report to the callback.

| Strategy | Cost | Requirements |
|---|---|---|
| `OnDiskMarkSweepStrategy` | Walks every retained version and scans the namespace's nodes | None |
| `RefcountGcStrategy` | Walks the retained and dropped versions, with no full scan | Versions recorded with `putRootWithRefcount`; only those are reclaimed |

### Retention policies

```java
RetentionPolicy.keepLatestN(10);
RetentionPolicy.keepVersions(List.of(1L, 5L, 10L));
RetentionPolicy.keepRange(5, 15);                // inclusive
```

A policy can also be any lambda from the roots index to the roots to keep.

### Rules

- **Stop writers first.** Don't run GC while anything else writes to the same namespace.
- **The latest root is always kept.** With a roots index, the `LATEST` root and the root at the last version survive whatever the policy says. Commit those tries before running GC, because a root visible only in an open write batch is rejected.
- **Without a roots index,** `OnDiskMarkSweepStrategy` keeps only the policy's roots.
- **Use one strategy per namespace,** and run mark-sweep occasionally to reclaim what refcount GC leaks.
- **Refcount GC fails safe.** It never deletes a node a retained version still reaches, even with wrong counts. It leaks instead and reports those nodes in `GcReport.protectedNodes`. It refuses to run when a retained root has no refcount.
- **Refcount GC edits the index.** It removes dropped versions from the roots index, while mark-sweep leaves the index as it is.

### After a crash

Both strategies use a temporary column family named `__vds_gc_marks_<digits>`. If you open the `RocksDB` yourself, open it with all column families from `RocksDB.listColumnFamilies` and call `GcManager.dropLeftoverGcColumnFamilies` after a crash.

### Databases written by 0.8.0-pre6 or earlier

0.8.0-pre7 fixed data-loss bugs in RocksDB GC, so upgrade before running GC on an existing database.

- Refcounts written by older code counted only roots. Refcount GC now protects retained tries from them and leaks instead of deleting.
- Temporary column families left by 0.8.0-pre6 are named `marks_<digits>` and are never dropped automatically. Check them, then drop them with `GcManager.dropLegacyGcColumnFamilies`.

For the algorithms and on-disk details, see the [GC design document](https://github.com/bloxbean/cardano-client-lib/blob/master/verified-structures/merkle-patricia-forestry-rocksdb/docs/gc.md).

---

# Overview

Source: https://cardano-client.dev/verified-structures/overview/
Summary: Merkle Patricia Forestry and Jellyfish Merkle Tree: authenticated data structures for Cardano applications.

> **Preview feature**: available in the [latest preview](/start-here/installation/#versions). APIs may change before the stable release.

A verified data structure stores key-value data off chain and reduces all of it to one hash, the *root*. Anyone who holds the root can check a *proof* that a key has a given value, or has no value, without having the data.

The usual Cardano pattern is to keep the data in your application, store the root in a datum, and let a validator check proofs on chain.

## Which one do I need?

| | [MpfTrie](/verified-structures/mpf/) | [Jellyfish Merkle Tree](/verified-structures/jmt/) |
|---|---|---|
| **Choose it for** | Proofs checked on chain by an Aiken validator | Versioned off-chain state, with proofs checked off chain |
| **On-chain verifier** | Aiken's `merkle-patricia-forestry` library | None |
| **Deleting a key** | Supported | Not implemented |
| **Reading old versions** | Record versions with a storage backend | Built in |
| **Writes** | One key at a time, or grouped in a session | Batches, each with a version number |

If your validator needs to check a proof, use MPF.

## Dependencies

RocksDB is the recommended storage. PostgreSQL, H2 and SQLite are alternatives, through the `-rdbms` modules. The storage modules bring in their core module.

```gradle
def cclVersion = '<version>' // the latest preview

dependencies {
    // MPF
    implementation "com.bloxbean.cardano:cardano-client-merkle-patricia-forestry-rocksdb:$cclVersion"

    // JMT
    implementation "com.bloxbean.cardano:cardano-client-jellyfish-merkle-rocksdb:$cclVersion"
}
```

SQL storage never creates its tables by itself. Call `RdbmsMpfSchema.createIfNotExists(dbConfig)` for MPF or `RdbmsJmtSchemaInstaller.createIfNotExists(dbConfig)` for JMT once, or apply the bundled DDL from `/ddl/{mpf,jmt}/{postgres,h2,sqlite}/schema.sql` with your migration tool. See the [MPF](https://github.com/bloxbean/cardano-client-lib/tree/master/verified-structures/merkle-patricia-forestry-rdbms) and [JMT](https://github.com/bloxbean/cardano-client-lib/tree/master/verified-structures/jellyfish-merkle-rdbms) module READMEs.

## Next steps

- [MpfTrie](/verified-structures/mpf/): store data and generate proofs for Aiken.
- [Jellyfish Merkle Tree](/verified-structures/jmt/): versioned state and proofs.
- [MPF versions and garbage collection](/verified-structures/multi-version-gc/) and the [MPF production guide](/verified-structures/production-guide/).

---

# MPF production guide

Source: https://cardano-client.dev/verified-structures/production-guide/
Summary: Atomic writes, RocksDB tuning, thread safety, backup and shutdown for MpfTrie.

> **Preview feature**: available in the [latest preview](/start-here/installation/#versions). APIs may change before the stable release.

## Atomic writes

`RocksDbMptSession` runs your work in one RocksDB write batch and commits it at the end. Nodes, the version entry and refcounts land together.

```java
import com.bloxbean.cardano.vds.mpf.rocksdb.RocksDbMptSession;

MpfTrie trie = new MpfTrie(stateTrees.nodeStore());
RocksDbMptSession session = RocksDbMptSession.of(stateTrees);

long version = session.write(() -> {
    trie.put("alice".getBytes(), "100".getBytes());
    trie.put("bob".getBytes(), "200".getBytes());
    return stateTrees.putRootWithRefcount(trie.getRootHash());
});
```

Inside a session, write only through the store APIs. A batch is bound to the calling thread.

For a bulk load that you can repeat, you can trade durability for speed by turning off the write-ahead log with `RocksDbMptSession.of(stateTrees, Options.builder().disableWal(true).build())`. Writes that aren't flushed yet are then lost on a crash or close, and they aren't in a backup.

## Storage layout

`RocksDbStateTrees` keeps two column families:

```text
nodes:  [ns][node hash]          -> CBOR-encoded node
        [ns][0xF0][node hash]    -> refcount (refcount GC only)
roots:  [ns][version]            -> root hash
        [ns]"LATEST"             -> latest root
        [ns]"VERSION"            -> last version number
        [ns]"_storage_mode"      -> MULTI_VERSION or SINGLE_VERSION
```

`[ns]` is the namespace's one-byte key prefix, `0x00` by default. To keep several tries in one database, pass `NamespaceOptions.keyPrefix((byte) 0x01)` or `NamespaceOptions.columnFamily("accounts")` to the constructor.

A RocksDB directory can be opened by only one `RocksDbStateTrees` at a time. Open namespaces one after another, or build `RocksDbNodeStore` and `RocksDbRootsIndex` instances over one shared `RocksDB` handle.

## RocksDB tuning

`RocksDbConfig` has the profiles `highThroughput()`, `balanced()`, `lowMemory()` and `defaults()`, plus a builder. Pass one to the constructor, and measure with your own workload:

```java
RocksDbStateTrees(String dbPath, NamespaceOptions namespace, StorageMode mode, RocksDbConfig config)
```

See the [rocksdb-core README](https://github.com/bloxbean/cardano-client-lib/tree/master/verified-structures/rocksdb-core) for its options.

## Thread safety

- `MpfTrie` isn't thread-safe. Use one instance per thread, or synchronize access.
- The backend has no concurrency control: serialize writers of a namespace.
- Pause writers while [garbage collection](/verified-structures/multi-version-gc/) runs. Its snapshot doesn't protect re-puts of existing node keys.

## Monitoring

```java
String stats = stateTrees.db().getProperty("rocksdb.stats");
String size = stateTrees.db().getProperty("rocksdb.total-sst-files-size");
```

## Backup and restore

Use RocksDB's own backup engine, with writers paused:

```java
try (BackupEngine backup = BackupEngine.open(Env.getDefault(), new BackupEngineOptions(backupPath))) {
    backup.createNewBackup(stateTrees.db(), true); // true flushes first
}

try (BackupEngine restore = BackupEngine.open(Env.getDefault(), new BackupEngineOptions(backupPath));
     RestoreOptions options = new RestoreOptions(false)) {
    restore.restoreDbFromLatestBackup(dbPath, dbPath, options);
}
```

## Shutdown

Close `RocksDbStateTrees`, ideally with try-with-resources. It closes the database and its resources.
